prompt: What is a virtual DOM?
hint: React builds one on every change.

choices.text: A second, hidden page that the browser renders off screen and then swaps in when it is ready
choices.why: It is not a page and the browser does not render it; it is plain JavaScript objects.

choices.text: A description of the page in JavaScript, rebuilt and compared after each change
choices.why: Right. The comparison is the diff, and applying it is the patch.

choices.text: The DOM the server builds while it renders, kept in memory until the HTML is sent to the visitor
choices.why: The server sends a string; the virtual DOM lives in the browser while the page runs.

choices.text: Svelte's name for the template its compiler writes
choices.why: Svelte has no virtual DOM. Its template is copied once, never compared.

prompt: Put React's steps after `setMinutes(30)` in order.
hint: The patch is last; the call to your function is first.
items: React compares it with the previous description
React changes the one text that differs
trap: Comparing needs the new description, so the call has to come before the diff.

prompt: Why did React adopt a virtual DOM in the first place?
hint: What is hard to write by hand?

choices.text: Because the browsers of 2013 had no DOM API that scripts could use
choices.why: They had one; using it precisely by hand was the problem.

choices.text: To let pages run without any JavaScript in the browser
choices.why: A virtual DOM is JavaScript running in the browser.

choices.text: Simple page code, with only the differences applied
choices.why: Right. The diff makes the simple way of writing affordable.

choices.text: Because the compiler it needed did not exist yet
choices.why: React never wanted a compiler for this; its components are plain functions on purpose.

prompt: Which cost of Svelte's design does React's design avoid?
hint: Think about who can read a component file.

choices.text: Tools have to understand Svelte syntax, since a `.svelte` file is not JavaScript
choices.why: Right. A React component is a plain function any JavaScript tool can read.

choices.text: Every change makes Svelte build a description of the page and compare it with the one before
choices.why: That is React's cost, not Svelte's.

choices.text: A Svelte app has to download the compiler before it can show the first page to a visitor
choices.why: The compiler runs on your computer at build time; the browser never gets it.

choices.text: Svelte touches more DOM nodes per change than React does
choices.why: Both end at the same single change; the section on counting showed it.

prompt: The counter's page was opened once and its button pressed three times. How many times did `the script ran` print in the browser?
hint: The script sets up; the effects respond.

choices.text: Four: once on load and once per press
choices.why: That was the effect. The script did not run again.

choices.text: Once
choices.why: Right. A component's script runs once, when it is created.

choices.text: Three, once per press
choices.why: Presses run effects, not the script.

choices.text: Twice: once to render and once to hydrate
choices.why: The second run was on the server, in the dev server's terminal, not in the browser.

prompt: After the page loaded and the button was pressed three times, how many `the effect ran` lines had the browser printed?
hint: One for appearing, then one per change.

prompt: Why did `the effect ran` never appear in the development server's terminal?
hint: What does the server do with the page once it is rendered?

choices.text: Because the server's console is switched off in development
choices.why: It is on: `the script ran` printed there.

choices.text: Because the effect failed silently on the server
choices.why: Nothing failed; effects are not run during server rendering at all.

choices.text: Effects do not run during server rendering, since nothing there changes after the string is sent
choices.why: Right. The server builds a string, sends it and forgets it.

prompt: `let hours = minutes / 60;` sits in the script, and the page shows `{hours}`. Pressing the button changes nothing on screen. Why?
hint: When did that line run, and how often?

choices.text: Dividing a `$state` value is not allowed and silently gives 0
choices.why: The division worked; it gave 0 because `minutes` was 0 at that moment.

choices.text: It ran once, when `minutes` was 0, and nothing runs it again
choices.why: Right, and the compiler warned with `state_referenced_locally`. `$derived` fixes it.

choices.text: The button's handler changes `hours` instead of `minutes`
choices.why: The handler adds to `minutes`, which did change; `hours` did not follow it.

choices.text: Hot replacement had not finished, so the old page was still showing
choices.why: `look` opens a fresh browser each time, so it saw the new component.

prompt: The compiler warning for reading a reactive value once, in a place that will never read it again, is `state_referenced____`.
hint: The last part says where it was referenced.

prompt: What is a signal?
hint: `$state` makes one.

choices.text: An event the browser fires when a value changes
choices.why: Browsers fire no such event; a signal is Svelte's own bookkeeping.

choices.text: A message the server sends to update the page
choices.why: Signals live in the browser's memory; the server is not involved.

choices.text: A value that keeps a list of the code that read it
choices.why: Right. A change goes down that list and nowhere else.

choices.text: A copy of a value kept to compare with the next one
choices.why: That is closer to what a virtual DOM keeps.

prompt: Pressing `Raise the goal` changed the second paragraph but did not print `the effect ran`. Why?
hint: Whose list is the logging effect on?

choices.text: The logging effect never read `goal`, so `goal`'s list does not include it
choices.why: Right. The paragraph has its own template effect, which did read `goal`.

choices.text: Effects only run for the first signal declared in a script
choices.why: Declaration order means nothing; reads decide.

choices.text: The button's handler ran before the effect had a chance to subscribe to anything
choices.why: The effect had run on load; it simply read `minutes` only.

choices.text: Console output is muted while a button is held down
choices.why: Nothing mutes the console; adding minutes printed straight after.

prompt: An effect reads `if (minutes > 0) console.log(`${minutes} of ${goal}`)`. With `minutes` at 0, you raise the goal. What prints?
hint: On its last run, did it read `goal`?

choices.text: `0 of 180`, since the effect mentions `goal`
choices.why: Mentioning is not reading: with `minutes` at 0 the line with `goal` never ran.

choices.text: Nothing; the effect does not depend on `goal` yet
choices.why: Right. An effect depends on exactly what it read the last time it ran.

choices.text: An error, because `goal` is read conditionally
choices.why: Conditional reads are allowed; they just make the dependency conditional too.

choices.text: `180`, since the compiler made the effect read every signal in the file
choices.why: Svelte 5 tracks reads at runtime; the compiler adds none.

prompt: Match each file with whether `$state` works in it.
hint: Runes are compiler words.

pairs.right: Works: a module the compiler reads
Fails: plain JavaScript, never compiled by Svelte

prompt: What does a `MutationObserver` report?
hint: It is a browser API, not Svelte's.

choices.text: Every time a signal changes value
choices.why: It knows nothing about signals; it watches the page.

choices.text: Each change made to the page: nodes, attributes, text
choices.why: Right, which is why it can count what a press touched.

choices.text: Each request the page sends to the server
choices.why: That is the network, which it does not watch.

choices.text: Errors thrown by scripts on the page
choices.why: Errors are reported elsewhere; `look` prints them as `error:` lines.

prompt: The page was opened and the buttons pressed three times in all. How many `changed:` lines did the observer print?
hint: One press, one change.

prompt: If the same observer watched a React version of the counter, what would it most likely report per press?
hint: Where does a virtual DOM end?

choices.text: Every node in the component, recreated
choices.why: The point of the diff is to avoid exactly that.

choices.text: Nothing, since React does not change the real DOM
choices.why: It does change it, at the end, in the patch.

choices.text: One text change, the same as Svelte
choices.why: Right. The difference is the work before it, not the change itself.

choices.text: The button and the paragraph, since they share a parent element
choices.why: Sharing a parent does not make the button change; its text never differs.

prompt: A page shows 3,000 rows and one of them changes. Where does Svelte's approach save work over a virtual DOM?
hint: Both end with the same DOM change.

choices.text: In the DOM change, which Svelte makes faster than the browser can
choices.why: Both make the same DOM change through the same browser.

choices.text: In finding the change: no descriptions of 3,000 rows rebuilt and compared
choices.why: Right. The effect for that row already knew what to set.

choices.text: In the download, since Svelte sends the rows already rendered
choices.why: Both can render on the server; the saving is at the moment of change.

prompt: Match each React habit with what replaces it in Svelte.
hint: Three come from the script running once.

pairs.right: Write the function; it is the same object for the component's life

prompt: Which React concern still applies in Svelte?
hint: Lesson 8 shows the wrong row keeping an input.

choices.text: Keeping hooks out of `if` statements
choices.why: Runes are compiler instructions, not calls counted in order.

choices.text: Giving list items a key
choices.why: Right. Without one, a reordered list is matched by position.

choices.text: Wrapping event handlers so children do not re-render
choices.why: Children do not re-render as a whole in Svelte; nothing to prevent.

choices.text: Copying arrays before changing them
choices.why: `$state` arrays are deep; changing them in place is tracked.

prompt: `let { minutes } = counter;` where `counter` is a `$state` object. Later `counter.minutes` changes. What does `minutes` hold?
hint: It is the same mistake as `hours`.

choices.text: The old number: destructuring copied it once
choices.why: Right. Read `counter.minutes` where you need it, or use `$derived`.

choices.text: The new number, since the object is reactive
choices.why: The object is; the local variable you copied into is not.

choices.text: `undefined`, since destructuring a proxy breaks it
choices.why: It copies the value that was there; nothing breaks.

choices.text: An error the first time `counter` changes
choices.why: No error: a stale copy is silent, which is why it is a trap.

prompt: What does Svelte give up in exchange for its small runtime?
hint: What has to happen before a `.svelte` file means anything?

choices.text: Server rendering, which needs a runtime
choices.why: Svelte renders on the server; lesson 1 compiled the server half.

choices.text: Reactivity for arrays and objects
choices.why: `$state` arrays and objects are deep and tracked.

choices.text: Being readable as plain JavaScript by any tool
choices.why: Right. Editors, linters and test runners have to know Svelte.

choices.text: The ability to run in browsers without a build step
choices.why: That is true but it is the same thing said differently; the cost named was the tools.

prompt: After the component is on the page, which of these run again when `minutes` changes? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only code that read `minutes` reacts.

choices.text: The template effect that shows `{minutes}`
choices.why: Yes: it read `minutes`.

choices.text: An `$effect` that logs `minutes`
choices.why: Yes: it read `minutes` on its last run.

choices.text: The component's `<script>`
choices.why: No: the script runs once.

choices.text: The template effect that shows `{goal}`
choices.why: No: it never read `minutes`.

prompt: Which sentence describes Svelte's reactivity correctly?
hint: Think of the list, and when it is built.

choices.text: The component re-runs and the output is compared
choices.why: That is React's.

choices.text: The compiler lists, once, every name that appears near each statement
choices.why: That was Svelte 4's `$:`; lesson 4 shows what it got wrong.

choices.text: Each signal records who read it at runtime, and a change reaches those readers
choices.why: Right.
